Not Roger Marshall! | | | Sep 19 | | | | | | | | | | | | I debated Sen. Marshall at the Kansas State Fair last week -- and the crowd made it clear they're ready for change. | | ---|---|--- One week ago, I took to the stage at the Kansas State Fair to debate Sen. Roger Marshall. We got into tariffs, the war in Iran and other corrupt and chaotic politics that are hurting people in Kansas and across the nation. The crowd was fired up, and so was I. I've listened to hundreds of Kansans talk about the problems they're facing. The struggle to afford groceries. The challenge of getting quality healthcare close to home. The fear of losing their businesses, their Social Security, their homes. That's why I was so eager for this debate. After listening to so many people, I have a plan to tackle the problems that corrupt politicians have created. Like I told the crowd, I'm ready to protect Kansas families from rising costs; end these disastrous tariffs; help end the war with Iran; defend Social Security; support Kansas farmers, ranchers and small-business owners; and fight against the chaos and corruption in Washington. Sen. Marshall, on the other hand? He's not ready to do any of that. How could he be? He's out of touch with what Kansans are struggling with because he doesn 't listen. More than 550 days ago, he got upset at a public town hall he held and walked out. After that, he refused to talk to Kansans because according to him, it's "dangerous" and "non-productive." But the crowd at our debate made sure he heard them anyway. And when the senator tried to defend suing more than 700 Kansans as "common business practices," the crowd chanted, "Shame on you." CNN called it "not a good moment for Roger Marshall." I would agree. In fact, "not good" might be an understatement. Folks, Kansas deserves a leader who will fight for Kansans -- not fight to make their ownlife better at Kansans ' expense. But maybe Sen. Marshall doesn't think he owes Kansans anything. After all, he spends a lot of his time in Florida, nearly 1,500 miles away from the people he represents! Folks, we Kansans are smart. We're tough. We believe in decency, respect and truth. When someone isn't being straight with us, we can tell. I think that's why, when Roger Marshall asked the crowd, "Who do you want solving this problem?" they immediately started chanting: "Not you!" The people who watched the debate can tell he's not interested in solving their problems. Under his watch, they've seen gasoline rise to $4.00/gallon and diesel hit a record-breaking $6.00+/gallon. They've witnessed tariffs drive up their cost of living and hurt their fellow farmers and manufacturers. They've watched while 51,000 people lost their Medicaid and 18,000 kids lost their SNAP benefits. Everywhere they turn, they 've seen Sen. Marshall fail them. And on Saturday, they called him to task for it. I know we can do better than Roger Marshall. It's time to retire him to Florida so we can start tackling the issues he's helped create. I can 't do it without your help, though. Unlike Sen. Marshall, I won't take a dime of corporate PAC money. That's why I depend on grassroots support from people like you. The debate showed Kansas and the country that the people of this great state are ready for a champion. Let 's keep the momentum going. name: Wes Moore
subject: I’m asking you to support a fellow Airborne officer
body:
He’s not a Democrat. Here’s why I’m backing him.
# [](https://act.wesmoore.com/go/8?t=1&akid=1955%2E1086043%2EQY-xTL)
Peter,
I want to tell you about someone I'm supporting for the United States Senate. He isn't a Democrat. I'm not asking him to become one. But I am asking you to help him anyway.
His name is Seth Bodnar, and he's running as an Independent in Montana. **[Today, I’m asking you to split a donation between our campaigns to help him win this Senate seat.](https://act.wesmoore.com/go/417?c0=wes-em-20260919-3.iYd1PG&refcode=em-20260919-3&t=2&akid=1955%2E1086043%2EQY-xTL)**
Before I was Governor of Maryland, I was a captain in the United States Army, with the 82nd Airborne Division in Afghanistan. Seth was an officer in the 101st Airborne who led an infantry platoon in Mosul, Iraq, and later served as a Green Beret.
We both went to Oxford as Rhodes Scholars. We both came home believing the same thing: that this country works best when people serve something bigger than themselves.
In the Army, nobody asks the soldier next to you what party they belong to. Your tribe isn’t red or blue; it’s red, white, and blue. **Your job is to show up for the person next to you when it counts.** Seth showed up for nineteen years in uniform, and then for eight years leading the University of Montana. Now, he is showing up for his state, when it would have been a lot easier not to.
The Republican nomination in Montana was handed to Kurt Alme eight minutes before the filing deadline. There was no real primary. No other Montanan got a say. Seth's answer was to collect nearly 30,000 signatures from voters in 52 counties and earn his place on the ballot the honest way. **Then a Trump-aligned Super PAC started spending millions attacking him.**
Seth is now gaining momentum faster than any candidate in that race. He's doing it without a party backing him. And in a Senate that's forgotten how to put country first, I'd like to see someone like Seth help us get back to solving the serious problems facing working people in this country.
**[So I’m asking: will you split a $10 donation between my campaign and Seth's to send a fellow Airborne officer to the United States Senate?](https://act.wesmoore.com/go/417?c0=wes-em-20260919-3.iYd1PG&refcode=em-20260919-3&t=3&akid=1955%2E1086043%2EQY-xTL)**

Montana deserves a senator who answers to Montana. I'm a Democrat, and I'm proud of it. But I'm prouder of the idea that service comes before party, and I'll back anyone who lives it.

clean_body: The SAVE America Act would suppress votes to address a made-up problem| | | | | | Donald Trump keeps demanding that Congress pass the SAVE America Act (the latest version of the anti-voting SAVE Act). With the House having passed it again, the Senate is all we have left to stop this suppressive legislation from becoming law ahead of the midterm elections , folks. Defenders of voting rights know that non-citizen voting is already illegal, extremely rare, and that this bill is written in a way that could disenfranchise millions of eligible women across the country. Here's Colorado Senator Michael Bennet on the impact of these bills: Opponents of voting rights in Congress -- and in the White House -- favor this new SAVE America Act because they know it could suppress millions of eligible voters, changing the composition of the electorate and potentially empowering them and their party for years to come. = If you've saved your payment information with ActBlue Express, your donation will go through immediately: | | | = | | = | | = | | | = | | = | | = | | | We know the SAVE America Act was fast-tracked by opponents of voting rights to be in place before November, folks. This bill is a stunning assault on our fundamental right to vote, and we can not afford to let this anti-democratic legislation become law. This bill would force every voter to present proof of citizenship to register, either a passport or a birth certificate that matches their current first and last name -- something millions of eligible American women don’t have. And that’s the point. The bill would also obliterate popular methods of voter registration for** all voters, including: Registration by mail 3rd party voter registration drives Online voter registration in states that allow it Automatic voter registration Some estimates say that this bill could disenfranchise anywhere from 11 million to 65 million eligible Americans , especially women and those who live in under-resourced communities. “ There’s never been an attack on voting rights out of Congress like this ,” said Alexander Keyssar, a professor of History and Social Policy at the Harvard Kennedy School, and a leading historian of voting rights. “ It’s always been the federal government trying to keep states in check on voting rights, for the most part. ” =** | | | | | | | ---|---|---|--- Integrity First Voter Action Project is dedicated to expanding ballot access and increasing voter participation across the country. This wasn't easy. | | | | Derek, MAGA Tom Tiffany is flooding the state with ads that lie about me. We need to respond. **That's why we just launched a new TV ad. We decided to invest even more money in it, including buying spots on tomorrow's Packers game.** This wasn't easy. With just a few weeks left in the race, we have such limited time to ensure we can afford this extra ad blitz. MAGA Tom Tiffany is raking in tons of money from a few far-right billionaire families. But if we meet our latest TV ad budget deadline, we'll have the resources to fund the buy when the banks open. We really don't want to have to pull back on our ad budget in the most crucial stretch. I know what another fundraising email can feel like, but I’m asking because a campaign rooted in Southwest Washington has to reach the people who live here. = I don’t take corporate PAC money. Keeping this seat belongs to ordinary people who believe a representative should answer to them. I have to ask you plainly for resources to reach voters and answer the outside spending headed our way. = | | | = I’d rather tell you why I’m asking than pretend the money won’t matter. Thanks for hearing me out. Marie = | | | | | ---|---|---|--- Congresswoman Marie Gluesenkamp Perez represents Washington’s 3rd Congressional District. * * *
One week after Charlie Kirk's memorial at UVU, Erika Kirk is finally going on the offensive.
This isn't a defamation suit, as most people expected. Instead, it's a lawsuit against the State of Utah for **[failing to protect Charlie Kirk](https://substack.com/redirect/c3521402-2515-4d96-bfe0-ceca65e947bd?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)** at Utah Valley University, a state school.
Many attorneys are signaling that Erika has an extremely strong case, and in her court documents, we find several bombshells regarding how the police failed to protect Charlie that day.
The first page of the court documents reads: "This document serves as a Notice of Claim against the State of Utah, Utah Valley University, the Utah Valley University Police Department, Jeffrey Long, Astrid Tuminez, and other state actors known and unknown."
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/0146a194-97ea-468b-86d9-34f47e16730c?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
Their argument? That UVU promised Charlie protection and failed. Erika Kirk's lawyers outlined six ways they failed in total:
**1\. Failure to understand the significance of Mr. Kirk 's visit to campus, which led to a lack of proper preparation.**
Kirk's lawyers cite a shocking admission from the UVU police: they did not have a security briefing before the event, despite it being one of the largest in their history. Officers also neglected to create a written security plan.
**2\. Deciding to permit the tour to take place in an outdoor venue without dedicating sufficient security resources to make that venue safe.**
UVU is aware of the complex layout of the area where they hosted Charlie on September 10. I have been to the crime scene multiple times, including last week, and the number of positions a sniper could find to take a lethal shot is extensive.
The state will surely argue that TPUSA ultimately decided to hold the event there. This is likely the weakest point in Kirk's intent to sue.
PolitiBrawl is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support our work, please consider becoming a paid subscriber.
[Upgrade to paid](https://substack..rmh7rUQ5FNhv6GORBRFbAJXRWmVvZDutBNe_VW64E4g?&utm_medium=email&utm_source=subscribe-widget-preamble&utm_content=216505861)
**3\. Assigning only six campus police officers to an outdoor event with thousands of attendees, despite requests for additional officers.**
Roughly 3,000 people were present at the Charlie Kirk event. That's one police officer per 500 people, representing only 25% of their total force. It will be difficult for the state to argue that UVU police weren't negligent on that point, especially given their long-standing partnership with the Orem Police, which could have afforded them more manpower.
**4\. Failing to exercise its exclusive power to keep Mr. Kirk safe.**
The police alone had the power to secure the UVU courtyard. While TPUSA had its own security, places with limited access, like rooftops, were the sole jurisdiction of UVU police. They also had unilateral authority to set up barriers and implement other crowd-control measures.
**5\. UVU put Mr. Kirk at additional risk by ignoring the specific tip it was given regarding the risk associated with rooftop access.**
TPUSA received a message from a student and forwarded it to the police chief in charge:
> "Hello Chief Long - we received this message today from the student group.... 'there is student roof access pretty close to where [Charlie Kirk] will be set up at Utah Valley (The Sorensen Student center has a couple of staircases that go up to the walkways on the roof). If this is true, it would be nice to either have it controlled access or allow one of my guys to be there as well. If Possible.'"
Chief Long assured TPUSA it would be secured... it was not. That roof was the very place Tyler Robinson shot Charlie Kirk from.
**6\. The UVU Parties ' omissions, actions, and misconduct led to Mr. Kirk's death.**
Erika Kirk's lawyers concluded that UVU should never hold any meeting or event on campus if they can't reasonably assume it is safe to do so.
### **Erika Kirk 's Timing**
Why drop the intent to sue now? The deadline to do so was one year after Charlie Kirk's assassination. This notice was filed on September 9th.
Erika Kirk and her legal team needed as much time as possible to conduct this investigation. They also likely didn't want to jeopardize the planned Charlie Kirk memorial event at UVU, which I attended.
With the case being as strong as it is, and with TPUSA being as busy as they are, I feel confident they will reach a settlement before it goes to trial.
Either way, we'll keep you updated as more lawsuits are sure to come.

It goes on to warn of “an unprecedented transformation of our economy, larger than the Industrial Revolution, but unfolding over a vastly shorter time frame,” with “risks, including large-scale job displacement.”| | | [](https://links.dpt.deepregimetrends.com/u/click?_t=4a25883d9bf54436b571b8aa9717dcca&_m=de52cac4e0594bedbc495aa5d3cb740c&_e=lptvs8mA3TFlQ58tHn6b_aKkHIjciXzhsmIO_3dFC7JfHYKMtQI7MxOaFXatPRn6UH-kcEeTyS7fUorzIXvDddLs55_yHNBV-0eV4HfV8Vtjdoq-KAiPWjsHcbnW_OrovM34qmq73QmuUmN9bw_q6fDKnYYyn7VvFhXcXLRHuyD_ZwnDmRISCg1-3MGWKI_0_Q1B3dSEDPfwdbC2EvDxmqNoboOcIoMeMKhbBdQzxqMXa27ElG19m5NNRrWXELMaiVU6TaWP-03F_cvfYD5LBHaFrWBZy2H7aojfcn1jhEPETFRyCLQUlvgFdE9BleDxmxjeEa3kpOcsNU4CAFbWvd9Hr3B7SNyv2Qp863ZFGLA%3D)

| | | | | On July 17, 1945, seventy of the scientists who built the atomic bomb signed a petition to the President of the United States.

They had spent three years building the thing.

Now they wanted Truman to hear, from them, what it was about to do.

**That letter never reached him.**

It sat in the chain of command until after Hiroshima, and it stayed classified until 1961.

**I bring this up because on July 13 of this year,** **it happened again.**

Just 88 words, posted on a website almost nobody visited.

**“AI may become radically more powerful over the next 10 years,”** it begins.

It goes on to warn of **“an unprecedented transformation of our economy, larger than the Industrial Revolution, but unfolding over a vastly shorter time frame,”** with **“risks, including large-scale job displacement.”**

17 Nobel Prize winners have signed that letter. Ben Bernanke. Paul Krugman. Robert Shiller. Joseph Stiglitz. Daron Acemoglu. Michael Spence.

[_But here’s what few people know, and fewer understand:_](https://links.dpt.deepregimetrends.com/u/click?_t=4a25883d9bf54436b571b8aa9717dcca&_m=de52cac4e0594bedbc495aa5d3cb740c&_e=lptvs8mA3TFlQ58tHn6b_dd6NhifJFz9LdPTUbAlpVg6J31rUxW5mD_-25OnGJJHfwr1kehJkHM0iRUkH0FH9QJDWztJcw_OX-uPiIQI8wueymLP82SAw1wX16_shJZAeJyzTpEm74XZEf7uBtQ7u6gHvioVX0of8424ON9baD2gzO4VqKuhzPGw2-dAPNgskl-3d2Ncjj6ma-sZQOvSpvkx39FESxfx9srcNQqeRE3SpeLAE_PJZNYonAXC7r2YmYNczGrHGpjaULglZJ7vAugwukJROybodxXoF9iuy9ToEv7vR6ZmQnmFPWsf5sxHxxb1Hzl19kT_rTPFs0THA20ahqIt76PNHjwpppt4Q-EvtM9MAcdbRQJMD3bny0DgepgrDtRznc8riR61PGhWq_S4WjOK3esdGlxYOCj5pK3S6lpGj8drQrujnE1kNaCQvLeM2vivzmDdgc2lqist3Q-yjFGDE20_au9oDoalHzaOOjndfrJLSmkCijU_kbZuDp19II5L2mjTCNDONhOViG4wurxtJ3F6R5ar4MRWvzk%3D)

Look further down the list of signatures. Sarah Friar, the chief financial officer of OpenAI. Jack Clark, a co-founder of Anthropic. Jeff Dean, Google’s chief scientist. Eric Schmidt. Reid Hoffman. Yann LeCun. Yoshua Bengio.

**Once again, the people building the machine signed a warning about the machine.**

That is the Szilárd moment.

I haven’t heard anyone on cable news read those 88 words aloud.

One of the economists who organized the letter, Anton Korinek, put the timeline in one sentence:
---
**“Steam, electricity, and computers each gave societies decades to adapt; AI may give us** _**only a few years.**_ **”**

Capital Rotation — September 19, 2026
The Price Fell. The Supply Cut Landed Somewhere Else.
Oil fell for a third day even as Aramco cut October crude entirely to European refiners — a sign the aggregate price and the underlying supply allocation are no longer telling the same story.
|
---
| | What Moved
---|---
**Verified fact:** oil fell for a third consecutive session Friday, with WTI and Brent both settling near $100.70, down roughly 1.2%–2.0% on the day. Equities were mixed — Dow -0.18%, S&P; 500 +0.17%, Nasdaq +0.39%. The 10-year Treasury yield rose back to 5.00%, and 2- and 3-year yields hit fresh 52-week highs.
| | Rotation Signal 01 — The Headline Oil Price and the Underlying Supply Picture Just Diverged
---|---
**Verified fact:** even as benchmark oil prices fell for a third day, Saudi Aramco informed at least two European refiners they will receive zero crude deliveries in October, affecting roughly 577,000 barrels a day of typical volume, after the East-West Pipeline's three damaged pumping stations were assessed at five to six weeks for full repair. **Our interpretation:** a falling benchmark price alongside a hard supply cut to specific customers suggests the broader market has priced in the Oman workaround's aggregate volume without yet fully pricing the uneven way that volume is being allocated — some buyers are being made whole, others are not, and the ones left out are the ones generating this week's least-visible headlines.
| | Rotation Signal 02 — The Yield Curve Sent a Different Signal Than Oil Did
---|---
**Our interpretation:** short-end Treasury yields (2- and 3-year) hitting 52-week highs on a day oil fell for the third straight session is not the combination markets would produce if they primarily saw this week's story as a resolving energy shock. It is more consistent with markets pricing the Fed's dot-plot signal of another 2026 hike as the dominant driver of near-term rates, with energy prices now a secondary input rather than the primary one they were two weeks ago.
| | Rotation Signal 03 — A Concrete, Multi-Billion-Dollar Signal About the War's Trajectory
---|---
**Verified fact:** the State Department approved a $24.3 billion sale of 48 F-35 stealth jets to Saudi Arabia. **Our interpretation:** unlike this week's rhetoric-heavy stories, a major defense sale is a slow-moving, hard-to-reverse commitment — a genuine data point about how the U.S. expects this conflict to run over years, not days. It signals continued, deepening material support for Saudi Arabia's own defense capacity, distinct from and likely more durable than any single week's diplomatic or rhetorical headline.
| | What to Watch Monday
---|---
Whether oil's three-day decline extends or reverses once markets fully digest Friday's European supply-cut news, and whether the short end of the yield curve continues to diverge from the energy narrative that dominated the first half of this month.

I need to reach out about an urgent concern that's been making headlines lately: the dire warnings coming from AI researchers.
As you've likely seen in the headlines, a researcher who worked inside both Anthropic and OpenAI, two of the companies building the most powerful AI models, recently issued a stark warning: Our ability to actually control these systems is diminishing - quickly.
The warnings extend beyond a couple of individuals: the leaders of three competing AI companies -- Anthropic's Dario Amodei, OpenAI's Sam Altman, and xAI's Elon Musk -- have all called for stronger guardrails on their own technology.
As a former computer programmer, I've spent my career thinking about what technology can build... and what it can break if we're not paying attention. AI has extraordinary potential: to solve complex problems, drive scientific breakthroughs, and improve people's lives. I want America to lead in this space, especially as we compete with China. But we can't overlook the risks that come alongside opportunity, and right now, the people closest to this technology are telling us the risks are real and accelerating.
**Congress cannot afford to sit back and watch.**
**That 's why I've called on Senate Commerce Committee Chairman Ted Cruz to immediately convene a hearing with testimony from the top executives of America's leading AI companies. We need them in front of Congress, on the record, answering hard questions about the pace of development and the safety guardrails -- or lack thereof -- that are supposed to keep Americans safe.**
This isn't a new fight for me. As a member of the Senate Commerce Committee, I've spent the last year pushing on exactly these issues:
* I pressed a Trump Administration official on why the government was deploying Grok, an AI chatbot with a documented history of promoting antisemitism, and I couldn't get a straight commitment that it wouldn't be used going forward.

* I raised concerns with the Federal Trade Commission about surveillance pricing: the practice of companies using AI to charge different people different prices for the exact same product, often without them ever knowing it's happening.

* And I introduced bipartisan legislation to keep DeepSeek, an AI platform with ties to the Chinese Communist Party, off of American government devices and networks, because our national security needs to come first.

Congress isn't known for moving at a rapid pace, unlike technological innovations. But if there was ever a moment to try to close that gap, it's now.
I'll keep pushing until that hearing happens.
Thanks for reading,
Jacky
* * *
##### `A personal note from Sen. Jacky Rosen:`
##### `My work in the Senate has always been defined by who I am and where I come from. Growing up as the granddaughter of immigrants and the daughter of a World War II veteran, my family instilled in me the values of hard work, determination, and persistence at a young age.`
##### `Now, I'm proud to fight tirelessly in the Senate to deliver progress for hardworking families like mine in Nevada and across our country. But with Donald Trump in the White House and Republicans in control of both houses of Congress, I need your grassroots support to keep up the fights that matter most.`
##### `Senate Democrats like me are the only thing standing in the way of Trump's extreme agenda that will hurt everyday Americans. That's why I need people like you on my side to help defend our progress and reclaim power from the GOP.`
##### `If you're with me, will you chip in now to help Democrats take back the Senate majority?`

body:
I’ll keep up this work — no matter how many Wawa runs it takes.
# [](https://act.sarahmcbride.com/go/1269?t=1&akid=3860%2E21716%2EGBecJB)
If you follow me on social media or read many of our emails, you probably know that I absolutely love coffee. **Especially when it comes from Wawa (sorry, not sorry Sheetz)!**
[](https://act.sarahmcbride.com/go/1184?c0=mcb-em-20260919-2.4H96A3&refcode=em20260919-3860&amount=5&t=2&akid=3860%2E21716%2EGBecJB)
While I take a quick coffee break, I wanted to reach out about something important: **we’re closing in on our — first and final — FEC end-of-quarter fundraising deadline of the general election, and it’s a big one.** [**And in addition to the coffee, I’m counting on your grassroots support to keep fueling this fight.**](https://act.sarahmcbride.com/go/1184?c0=mcb-em-20260919-2.4H96A3&refcode=em20260919-3860&amount=5&t=3&akid=3860%2E21716%2EGBecJB)
Because while folks keep asking me about cream and sugar, they're also talking about the real issues — like how to bring down the cost of housing and groceries, how to make childcare more affordable, and how to visit the doctor without breaking the bank. They want to know someone is fighting for them, as Donald Trump and corrupt DC Republicans rip us off and pad the pockets of billionaires.
That’s what I’m focused on every day in Congress. I’m showing up, speaking out, and fighting to make sure my neighbors and working families everywhere have a fair shot — no matter how many Wawa runs it takes!
**But here’s the truth: Delaware’s primary election was the last in the country, which means we have _less than 7 weeks_ to build a general election campaign. On top of that, I am legally required to report our fundraising numbers to the Federal Election Commission on September 30 **— it’s our only chance before Election Day to show the strength of our grassroots movement before voters start casting their ballots.
Raising enough resources to post a strong report is essential to help me stay in Congress and build the coalition we need to take back the House.
[**So if you’re with me, will you pitch in $5 or more to support my General Election campaign? I can’t defend Delaware’s seat in Congress without you.**](https://act.sarahmcbride.com/go/1184?c0=mcb-em-20260919-2.4H96A3&refcode=em20260919-3860&amount=5&t=4&akid=3860%2E21716%2EGBecJB)
Thank you so much,
Sarah McBride

They want to know someone is fighting for them, as Donald Trump and corrupt DC Republicans rip us off and pad the pockets of billionaires. That’s what I’m focused on every day in Congress. I’m showing up, speaking out, and fighting to make sure my neighbors and working families everywhere have a fair shot — no matter how many Wawa runs it takes! But here’s the truth: Delaware’s primary election was the last in the country, which means we have less than 7 weeks to build a general election campaign. On top of that, I am legally required to report our fundraising numbers to the Federal Election Commission on September 30 — it’s our only chance before Election Day to show the strength of our grassroots movement before voters start casting their ballots. Raising enough resources to post a strong report is essential to help me stay in Congress and build the coalition we need to take back the House. Thank you so much, Sarah McBride

[**_If you care about flipping North Carolina, Roy needs your immediate support right now: Will you chip in $5 or more directly to Roy Cooper’s campaign?_**](https://act.roycooper.com/go/15912?refcode=email_fr_pros_jtk1392&amount=5&t=8&akid=3627%2E124072%2EIAuFlD)

The spending in North Carolina’s U.S. Senate race is reaching a fever pitch.

_**Cliff 's Note:**_
##### Eric Lullove is our contributing medical editor. He is a board-certified surgeon who runs a wound-healing center in Florida, and in August he wrote the only piece anywhere in progressive media about a line buried in a Medicare rule that is about to punish the sickest patients in the country. He reads the regulations. That is why he is here.
##### What he sent me this week is not a health policy article. It is a physician saying that the last year and a half is showing up in his exam room -- in blood pressure, in sleep, in A1c numbers on people who are doing everything right -- and that he has stopped being able to treat it as background noise.
##### There is a paragraph in the middle of it I have not stopped thinking about. He says he now checks federal health data against state health departments before he believes it. A doctor said that. About the CDC.
##### Read it and then go check your registration.
[Upgrade to paid](https://substack.com/redirect/2/eyJlIjoiaHR0cHM6Ly93d3cuYmx1ZWFtcC5jby9zdWJzY3JpYmU_.zwwPMI5AtTT-0dILQ_5uZkg_4Ysv5D8_jD9XIbm4aZI?&utm_medium=email&utm_source=subscribe-widget&utm_content=216509350)
_**-- Cliff**_
* * *
## Why Elections Matter
Some version of the same conversation happens in my exam room every week. A patient's blood pressure is up. Their sleep is broken. Their A1c has crept up despite doing everything right. When I ask what changed, the answer increasingly has nothing to do with diet or medication. It's the rent. It's the grocery bill. It's the twice-a-week filling up the car with gas. It's the benefit letter they don't understand. It's the feeling that the people running this country are lying to them, profiting off them, and that there's nothing they can do about it.
This isn't an article about health care policy. It's about something more basic: the choices made in Washington right now are medical and psychological events. They enter our bloodstream. And the decisions of this administration and the people it has placed atop our federal agencies are producing a chronic, population-wide stress response that I, as a physician, can no longer treat as background noise.
## The Body Keeps the Ballot
The late neuroendocrinologist Bruce McEwen called it allostatic load: the cumulative wear and tear of chronic stress. Acute stress is survivable. The body spikes cortisol, adapts, and recovers. Chronic stress never lets the system reset. The result is hypertension, insulin resistance, inflammation, suppressed immunity, cognitive decline, and depression.
What I'm about to describe is allostatic load administered by policy, at national scale.

## Corruption and Grift: A Tax on Hope
Public health research, including Ichiro Kawachi's work on social capital, has long linked social trust to lower mortality. When people believe the system is fair, they plan, invest in the future, and seek help. When they believe it's rigged, they stop.
Now consider what Americans have watched in the past year and a half. According to a 927-page financial disclosure report filed with the Office of Government Ethics, President Trump and his family earned more than $1 billion last year through cryptocurrency ventures and other businesses. A Reuters investigation published in June found the family made $2.3 billion from four cryptocurrency ventures through the end of April 2026 while putting up little to no capital of their own, and outside investors lost an equivalent $2.3 billion in the same projects. More than $250 million of the new crypto firm's revenue came from an investor tied to United Arab Emirates royalty. Days after a UAE sovereign fund's $2 billion investment in the family's stablecoin, the administration granted the UAE broader access to U.S. AI chips.
The material harm is money flowing to the connected. The psychological harm is worse: a nation watching the presidency function as a business opportunity learns that effort is for suckers and the rules are for other people. Anne Case and Angus Deaton named where that road ends: deaths of despair, from overdose, suicide, and alcohol. Grift doesn't just steal money. It steals the belief that playing fair pays.
## Lies: When the Truth Becomes a Political Variable
Here is a lie with a body count.
Pennsylvania is in the grip of the worst measles outbreak in decades. As of September 15, the Pennsylvania Department of Health had confirmed 693 cases in 38 counties, with 133 hospitalizations and four measles-associated deaths. HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has said that only one of the earlier deaths was directly linked to the infection. The CDC has not counted any measles deaths in 2026, and the decision to exclude Pennsylvania's reported deaths from its weekly update came from the agency's new director, Dr. Erica Schwartz. And on the very day I'm writing this, Kennedy delivered the keynote at a Washington conference hosted by Children's Health Defense, a vaccine-skeptic group, telling them they have "a friend in the White House" in President Trump.
The downstream effect is measurable. A Reuters/Ipsos poll in September 2026 found 76 percent of Americans considered the MMR vaccine safe for children, down from 84 percent in a comparable May 2020 survey, while national kindergarten vaccination rates have fallen below the 95 percent threshold needed to maintain herd immunity.
I want to be honest with you about something. I have spent my career practicing evidence-based medicine. For decades, the CDC, FDA, and CMS were the bedrock that evidence stood on. I didn't always agree with them, but I trusted that their data was real and their guidance was made in good faith. I can't say that anymore. As a scientist, I now check federal health data against state health departments, independent researchers, and investigative reporting before I believe it. That is what moral injury looks like from inside the profession. And if a physician feels it, imagine what it's doing to the parent in Lancaster County trying to decide whether measles is a real threat to her child.
Psychologists define moral injury as the wound that forms when the institutions you depend on betray their own mission. When the nation's health secretary and its disease-control agency become the source of confusion rather than clarity, every parent in America absorbs that injury. And a Finnish cohort study in Neurology found that people with high levels of cynical distrust had higher rates of dementia and death. Lies don't just degrade the discourse. Over time, the distrust they breed degrades us.
## Safety-Net Cuts and the Reduction of Services
The safety net is a budget line in Washington. In the body, it's a stress buffer. The Oregon Health Insurance Experiment found that giving low-income adults coverage cut depression rates by roughly 30 percent, driven largely by removing the fear of financial catastrophe. Food insecurity tracks with depression and anxiety. Eviction tracks with maternal depression that lasts for years.
This administration and its congressional allies are pulling that buffer away. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act set in motion the largest cuts to Medicaid in the program's history, roughly $1 trillion over ten years.18,19 The Congressional Budget Office estimates the law will increase the number of uninsured Americans by 10 million in 2034, 7.5 million of them because of its Medicaid provisions.
Medicaid eligibility redeterminations shift from annual to every six months beginning October 1, 2026, and work and reporting requirements for Medicaid expansion adults take effect January 1, 2027.19 The Congressional Budget Office also estimates the law cuts SNAP by nearly $187 billion through 2034, the largest cut in the program's history, removing more than 2.4 million people from the program in a typical month.
Read that renewal schedule again with a clinician's eye. Every six months, millions of the poorest and sickest Americans will face a paperwork test where failure means losing care. That is a recurring, state-scheduled stressor, designed into law.
## Judicial Decisions: The Longest Half-Life in Politics
Presidents serve four years. The judges they appoint serve for decades, and their rulings shape the conditions of life long after the campaign ends.
This year showed both faces of that power. In a sharp rebuke to President Trump, the Supreme Court ruled 6-3 that the Constitution guarantees automatic birthright citizenship, firmly rejecting the executive order he issued on the first day of his second term. That's what a working check looks like. But the Court also allowed Alabama to keep its 2026 elections using a map with districts a lower court had found to be racially discriminatory, the first test of Louisiana v. Callais, which substantially raised the bar for proving Voting Rights Act violations. That map eliminates a majority-Black voting district, scattering its residents over three districts.
Think about what that does to a voter's psyche: being told your vote was diluted, a court agreed, and it's happening anyway. That is learned helplessness delivered by judicial order.
## Bad Policy: The Slow Poison
Some harm isn't ideological. It's institutional demolition. Last September, senators questioned Kennedy over his termination of CDC Director Susan Monarez, who had been confirmed by the Senate. In his own budget testimony, Kennedy projected saving an estimated $1.8 billion per year beginning in fiscal 2026 through a reduction in the HHS workforce. Fewer epidemiologists, fewer inspectors, fewer people answering the phone. Bad policy rarely announces itself. It shows up years later, in someone's bloodwork, or in a county coroner's report.
## Now I Want to Ask You Something
Stop reading for a moment and take your own history.
How are you sleeping? When you open the news in the morning, what happens in your chest? Do you feel anger? Dread? A numbness you didn't have five years ago? Have you caught yourself thinking that nothing you do matters, that they'll do what they want regardless, so why bother?
I want you to name it, because naming a symptom is the first step to treating it. And I want you to notice something about that last feeling, the why bother. It isn't a personal failing. It's a textbook clinical response, and it has a name.

More than $250 million of the new crypto firm's revenue came from an investor tied to United Arab Emirates royalty. Days after a UAE sovereign fund's $2 billion investment in the family's stablecoin, the administration granted the UAE broader access to U.S. AI chips. The material harm is money flowing to the connected. The psychological harm is worse: a nation watching the presidency function as a business opportunity learns that effort is for suckers and the rules are for other people. Anne Case and Angus Deaton named where that road ends: deaths of despair, from overdose, suicide, and alcohol. Grift doesn't just steal money. It steals the belief that playing fair pays. Lies: When the Truth Becomes a Political Variable Here is a lie with a body count. Pennsylvania is in the grip of the worst measles outbreak in decades. As of September 15, the Pennsylvania Department of Health had confirmed 693 cases in 38 counties, with 133 hospitalizations and four measles-associated deaths. HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has said that only one of the earlier deaths was directly linked to the infection. The CDC has not counted any measles deaths in 2026, and the decision to exclude Pennsylvania's reported deaths from its weekly update came from the agency's new director, Dr. Erica Schwartz. And on the very day I'm writing this, Kennedy delivered the keynote at a Washington conference hosted by Children's Health Defense, a vaccine-skeptic group, telling them they have "a friend in the White House" in President Trump. The downstream effect is measurable. A Reuters/Ipsos poll in September 2026 found 76 percent of Americans considered the MMR vaccine safe for children, down from 84 percent in a comparable May 2020 survey, while national kindergarten vaccination rates have fallen below the 95 percent threshold needed to maintain herd immunity. I want to be honest with you about something. I have spent my career practicing evidence-based medicine. For decades, the CDC, FDA, and CMS were the bedrock that evidence stood on. I didn't always agree with them, but I trusted that their data was real and their guidance was made in good faith. I can't say that anymore. As a scientist, I now check federal health data against state health departments, independent researchers, and investigative reporting before I believe it. That is what moral injury looks like from inside the profession. And if a physician feels it, imagine what it's doing to the parent in Lancaster County trying to decide whether measles is a real threat to her child. Psychologists define moral injury as the wound that forms when the institutions you depend on betray their own mission. When the nation's health secretary and its disease-control agency become the source of confusion rather than clarity, every parent in America absorbs that injury. And a Finnish cohort study in Neurology found that people with high levels of cynical distrust had higher rates of dementia and death. Lies don't just degrade the discourse. Over time, the distrust they breed degrades us. Safety-Net Cuts and the Reduction of Services The safety net is a budget line in Washington. In the body, it's a stress buffer. The Oregon Health Insurance Experiment found that giving low-income adults coverage cut depression rates by roughly 30 percent, driven largely by removing the fear of financial catastrophe. Food insecurity tracks with depression and anxiety. Eviction tracks with maternal depression that lasts for years. This administration and its congressional allies are pulling that buffer away. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act set in motion the largest cuts to Medicaid in the program's history, roughly $1 trillion over ten years.18,19 The Congressional Budget Office estimates the law will increase the number of uninsured Americans by 10 million in 2034, 7.5 million of them because of its Medicaid provisions. Medicaid eligibility redeterminations shift from annual to every six months beginning October 1, 2026, and work and reporting requirements for Medicaid expansion adults take effect January 1, 2027.19 The Congressional Budget Office also estimates the law cuts SNAP by nearly $187 billion through 2034, the largest cut in the program's history, removing more than 2.4 million people from the program in a typical month. Read that renewal schedule again with a clinician's eye. Every six months, millions of the poorest and sickest Americans will face a paperwork test where failure means losing care. That is a recurring, state-scheduled stressor, designed into law. Judicial Decisions: The Longest Half-Life in Politics Presidents serve four years. The judges they appoint serve for decades, and their rulings shape the conditions of life long after the campaign ends. This year showed both faces of that power. In a sharp rebuke to President Trump, the Supreme Court ruled 6-3 that the Constitution guarantees automatic birthright citizenship, firmly rejecting the executive order he issued on the first day of his second term. That's what a working check looks like. But the Court also allowed Alabama to keep its 2026 elections using a map with districts a lower court had found to be racially discriminatory, the first test of Louisiana v. Callais, which substantially raised the bar for proving Voting Rights Act violations. That map eliminates a majority-Black voting district, scattering its residents over three districts. Think about what that does to a voter's psyche: being told your vote was diluted, a court agreed, and it's happening anyway. That is learned helplessness delivered by judicial order. Bad Policy: The Slow Poison Some harm isn't ideological. It's institutional demolition. Last September, senators questioned Kennedy over his termination of CDC Director Susan Monarez, who had been confirmed by the Senate. In his own budget testimony, Kennedy projected saving an estimated $1.8 billion per year beginning in fiscal 2026 through a reduction in the HHS workforce. Fewer epidemiologists, fewer inspectors, fewer people answering the phone. Bad policy rarely announces itself. It shows up years later, in someone's bloodwork, or in a county coroner's report. Now I Want to Ask You Something Stop reading for a moment and take your own history. How are you sleeping? When you open the news in the morning, what happens in your chest? Do you feel anger? Dread? A numbness you didn't have five years ago? Have you caught yourself thinking that nothing you do matters, that they'll do what they want regardless, so why bother? I want you to name it, because naming a symptom is the first step to treating it. And I want you to notice something about that last feeling, the why bother. It isn't a personal failing. It's a textbook clinical response, and it has a name. Continue reading this post for free in the Substack app | | | | | | | (C) 2026 Cliff Schecter PO Box 8384, Cincinnati, OH 45208 ? ?

This news
isn’t a surprise.

Earlier this week The Cook Political Report changed its rating for New
Hampshire’s Senate race from Lean Democrat to Toss Up.

[ https://act.chrispappas.org/go/181?c0=em_ms_cp_20260919_3.6eAgOh&refcode=em20260919-3&t=1003&akid=9026%2E582294%2EoSows6 ]Washington Post Logo[ https://act.chrispappas.org/go/181?c0=em_ms_cp_20260919_3.6eAgOh&refcode=em20260919-3&t=1004&akid=9026%2E582294%2EoSows6 ]Washington Post: This blue state is the midterms'
surprising new Senate battleground

This is exactly the update Republicans were waiting for.

They’ve been pouring millions of dollars into New Hampshire for months in
an effort to flip this seat — knowing this could be their best shot at
holding onto the Senate majority.

Here’s the thing: A race doesn’t shift to Toss Up without pressure from
the other side.

It didn’t happen because our support isn’t strong. It happened because
Republicans are spending early and aggressively, hedging their bets that
we won’t be able to keep pace.

I’m no stranger to difficult fights, but I can’t win this one
alone. I’m going to need a flood of grassroots support to cross the finish
line in just 45 days.

That’s why I’m asking you today: [ https://act.chrispappas.org/go/181?c0=em_ms_cp_20260919_3.6eAgOh&refcode=em20260919-3&t=1006&akid=9026%2E582294%2EoSows6 ]Will you chip in $5
today to help make sure we have everything we need heading towards
November?

[ https://act.chrispappas.org/go/181?c0=em_ms_cp_20260919_3.6eAgOh&amount=5&refcode=em20260919-3&t=1025&akid=9026%2E582294%2EoSows6 ]Donate $5 »

Thank you,

Chris Pappas
